name: Artificial basin irrigation, Nile valley
summary: Egyptian farmers improved the Nile's natural flood basins with feeder canals and dykes, and canal work is depicted at the start of unified Egypt around 3100 BCE.
description: Farmers along the Egyptian Nile first relied on natural flood-recession basins. Manning describes artificial irrigation as an improvement of that system by feeder and drainage canals and by transverse dykes that divided the basins into smaller units, and takes the Scorpion macehead, read as a king clearing a canal about 3100 BCE, as its earliest attestation. The macehead shows canal work; which of the other works existed at that date is not shown.

impact.note: One society, the Egyptian Nile valley, lived by it; the source presents it as an improvement of existing flood-recession farming rather than a new basis of life, and the Old Kingdom canals it mentions are the few successors shown.

date.label: by c. 3100 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Manning says artificial irrigation of the fields is attested at the very beginning of unified Egyptian history, citing the Scorpion macehead, which he reads as showing the king clearing a canal about 3100 BCE.

evidence.supports: Such artificial irrigation of the fields is attested at the every beginning of unified Egyptian history (The so-called “Scorpion Macehead” depicting the king clearing a canal ca. 3100 BC)

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The source is a specialist's draft paper; the ca. 3100 BC date and the canal reading of the Scorpion macehead are given without a primary citation and should be checked against the macehead's publication.
Whether basins divided by transverse dykes existed at this date, or only canals, is not settled by the source read.
Butzer's two models of how artificial irrigation developed (2001) and his 1976 book were not read; the scanned copy of the book could not be read by the fetcher.
Whether Egyptian irrigation arose without influence from Mesopotamia is not addressed by the source read.

research.note: Manning describes artificial irrigation as an improvement of the local natural flood-basin system, and the sources read do not say whether it arose without contact with Mesopotamia, so independence is not established.
